candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: An endless future never contains an actually infinite number of completed events, even if there is no later standpoint from which the whole process is surveyed.
candidates.attributionBasis: The turn directly states Craig's own denial and follows Malpass's explicit discussion of Bill's position.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This preserves Craig's asymmetry between an endless potential future and a completed actual infinite, which is central to answering the future-parity objection.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Malpass's claim that Craig illicitly moves from simple-future claims to future-perfect claims about completing an infinite count.

candidates.contextSummary: Malpass had argued that an infinite future can contain all counting events without there ever being a future time at which the count has been completed; Craig denies that an actual infinite ever results.

candidates.speaker: Alex Malpass
candidates.proposition: Craig's reverse-countdown discussion appears to contain a distinct impossibility argument: at every earlier time the counter supposedly should already have finished, leaving no time at which counting occurs.
candidates.attributionBasis: Malpass introduces the reverse-countdown topic, describes Craig's published reasoning, and explicitly offers his own analysis of it.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The reverse-countdown scenario is a direct formulation of the successive-addition case against a beginningless past, and Malpass isolates the inference on which its alleged impossibility depends.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's reverse-countdown argument that a person counting from infinity should already have finished at every earlier point.

candidates.contextSummary: After setting aside their dispute about future counting, Malpass turns to the past-directed analogue and distinguishes an explanatory objection from an argument that the countdown could never be underway.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: If having infinitely much time and a one-to-one correspondence suffices to finish a reverse countdown, the counter should have finished at every earlier time, contradicting the hypothesis that he counted eternally.
candidates.attributionBasis: Craig explicitly identifies the reasoning as a dialectical argument and develops each stage in the first person as his own position.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is Craig's direct defense of a successive-addition argument against a beginningless sequence, culminating in an internal contradiction for the proposed eternal countdown.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Malpass's suggestion that Craig's explanatory and already-finished considerations are separate arguments whose relationship is unclear.

candidates.contextSummary: Craig explains that the countdown puzzle, the sufficient-condition response, the regress to earlier completion times, and a modest explanatory principle are successive stages of one dialectic.

candidates.speaker: Alex Malpass
candidates.proposition: Infinitely many prior counting events are necessary for finishing a reverse countdown now but are not sufficient, so they do not imply that the counter should have finished earlier.
candidates.attributionBasis: Malpass explicitly divides Craig's account into parts and states his own necessary-versus-sufficient-condition objection.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The objection targets the key modal inference in Craig's reverse-countdown reasoning and, if successful, blocks the claimed contradiction without denying an infinite past.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's inference from the counter's having infinitely much prior time to the conclusion that he should already have completed the countdown.

candidates.contextSummary: Malpass accepts that finishing now entails infinitely many prior counts but argues that the converse fails because an eternal counter could presently have any finite number still remaining.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: An infinite amount of time paired one-to-one with the numbers leaves nothing further needed for completion, unless one denies any explanatory requirement for why completion occurs at one time rather than another.
candidates.attributionBasis: Craig answers immediately after Malpass's modal objection and frames the sufficiency and explanatory claims as his own reasoning.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This directly supplies Craig's defense of the disputed sufficiency premise and connects the reverse-countdown contradiction to a modest principle of sufficient reason.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Malpass's claim that infinitely many elapsed counting events make present completion possible but do not make earlier completion necessary.

candidates.contextSummary: Craig responds that infinite time plus the stipulated correspondence appears sufficient for finishing and says the remaining escape requires rejecting an explanation for the selected completion time.

candidates.speaker: Alex Malpass
candidates.proposition: A modest partial explanation can account for finishing now—such as having ten numbers left ten minutes ago and counting one per minute—even if it does not explain the entire infinite history.
candidates.attributionBasis: Malpass discusses Craig's cited principle, develops an extended account of partial explanation, and applies it directly to the countdown.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move challenges Craig's explanatory fallback by offering the kind of non-entailing, mystery-displacing explanation that a modest principle of sufficient reason appears to require.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's contention that an eternal countdown offers no adequate explanation for finishing today instead of at an earlier time.

candidates.contextSummary: Malpass distinguishes partial explanation from an entailment-producing total explanation, illustrates the distinction with a causal chain, and then gives a local rate-based explanation of completion.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: The relevant modest principle of sufficient reason is defensible yet still violated by a countdown that finishes at one point rather than another, because no adequate explanation selects that point.
candidates.attributionBasis: Craig repeatedly refers to his published defense and directly states that the proposed countdown violates the principle used there.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This maintains the explanatory component of Craig's reverse-countdown case after Malpass offers a local partial explanation and identifies the precise alleged defect in the scenario.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Malpass's proposed partial explanation that the counter finishes now because ten numbers remained ten minutes earlier at a fixed counting rate.

candidates.contextSummary: Craig does not reconstruct the published principle from memory, but insists that its modest formulation is plausible and that an eternal countdown cannot explain its particular completion point.

candidates.speaker: Alex Malpass
candidates.proposition: Grim Reaper arguments do not presently provide a settled objection because their beginning-of-time reasoning may be temporally mirrored to imply that the future must also have an end.
candidates.attributionBasis: The question is directed to Malpass, who identifies his current research interest and expressly withholds confidence in the mirrored argument.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The proposed temporal mirror bears directly on whether an infinity-based paradox supports a beginning asymmetrically or instead generates an unacceptable parallel conclusion about the future.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The audience question invoking Pruss's Grim Reaper and Hilbert's Hotel argument against a backwards-infinite sequence of events.

candidates.contextSummary: Malpass cannot identify a premise-by-number response on the spot, refers to related work on accumulation, and emphasizes a possible future-directed mirror of the Grim Reaper reasoning.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: Causal finitism breaks the alleged past-future parallel because no event may have infinitely many causes, excluding a beginningless causal past without excluding an endless forward causal series.
candidates.attributionBasis: Craig presents Pruss's causal-finitist argument approvingly and clearly states both its prohibition and its asymmetric consequences.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument offers an alternative philosophical route to a finite past that directly answers Malpass's symmetry objection while allowing the future to remain endless.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Malpass's suggestion that Grim Reaper-style arguments for a temporal beginning can be mirrored to establish an end of the future.

candidates.contextSummary: Craig recommends Pruss's causal-finitist treatment as a way to avoid temporal parallelism by imposing finitude on the causal ancestry of an event rather than on every temporal series.

candidates.speaker: Alex Malpass
candidates.proposition: Malpass's position is skeptical rather than beginningless-past advocacy: dismantling arguments that the universe began does not establish that the universe had no beginning.
candidates.attributionBasis: In direct response to a question about his strongest objections, Malpass explicitly characterizes the scope and limits of his own position.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This clarifies the con side's exact burden on the motion: the critique contests whether the infinity arguments adequately support a beginning, not whether a beginning is false.
candidates.contextSummary: Malpass says his most plausible objections disarm positive beginning arguments; he offers no positive case for an infinite past and regards familiar arguments against a beginning as implausible.
